content.title: About
content.content: Baklava is a traditional Middle Eastern dessert made of many thin layers of phyllo dough, a nut filling (usually walnuts, pistachios or almonds) and a fragrant syrup or honey infused with spices such as cinnamon and clove.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baklava dates back to the Ottoman Empire and is mentioned in culinary texts from the 15th century.
There are numerous regional variations—Turkish, Greek, Armenian, Lebanese—each differing in nut type and syrup preparation.
Phyllo sheets are rolled out so thin that light can pass through them.
Traditionally baklava is cut into diamonds or squares, though some cultures shape it into rolls.
It is often said that baklava tastes best the next day, when the syrup has fully soaked the layers.

items.title: Nut‑rich source
items.content: The nuts provide healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, protein, B‑vitamins and minerals such as magnesium and phosphorus.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Nuts and spices like cinnamon and clove contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Baklava quickly replenishes energy thanks to its high carbohydrate and fat content, useful in cold weather or after physical activity.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Polyunsaturated fatty acids in the nuts may help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: Nuts and the whole‑grain phyllo contribute a modest amount of dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Baklava contains nuts, which can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The syrup or honey makes the dessert very sweet, which can be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching their sugar intake.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Baklava is rich in calories from fats and carbs, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some commercial versions use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats; choose products made with real butter when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baklava is usually served at room temperature, cut into bite‑size pieces. It can be enjoyed on its own or paired with tea or coffee, and some people drizzle extra honey over it before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baklava in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. At room temperature it stays fresh for 3‑4 days; for longer storage (up to 2‑3 weeks) keep it in the refrigerator and bring it back to room temperature before serving.
